w: Elvis Presley bought this Whitehaven mansion and lived here until his death in 1977; he's buried in the grounds alongside his parents and daughter Lisa Marie. Opened to the public in 1982, it now draws some 600,000 visitors a year - second only to the White House among American homes.
s: Elvis's home, second most-visited house in the US
_facts: 13.8-acre Whitehaven estate owned by Elvis Presley
Elvis, parents Vernon and Gladys, grandmother, grandson, and daughter Lisa Marie all buried there
Opened as house museum 1982; ~600,000 visitors/year, second most visited US home after the White House
First rock-music site on National Register (1991); National Historic Landmark 2006

w: Founded in 1916 and tucked into Overton Park, the Brooks holds the title of oldest and largest art museum in Tennessee - a privately funded nonprofit that's outlasted plenty of grander civic ambitions elsewhere in Midtown Memphis. No state money, no fuss, just one of the South's deeper permanent collections.
s: Tennessee's oldest and largest art museum
_facts: Founded 1916
Oldest and largest art museum in Tennessee
Privately funded nonprofit institution
Located in Overton Park, Midtown Memphis

w: Built in 1917 to carry two rail lines across the Mississippi to Arkansas, with roadways cantilevered off its sides for cars until a newer bridge took over in 1949. Those roadways sat unused for decades until 2016, when they reopened as a pedestrian and bike crossing - the country's second-longest.
s: A century-old rail bridge reborn as a walkway
_facts: Cantilevered through-truss bridge, built 1917 across the Mississippi to West Memphis, AR
Carries two rail lines; roadways for vehicles used 1917-1949
Owned/operated by Union Pacific Railroad
Converted 2011-2016 into a bicycle-pedestrian walkway; second-longest pedestrian bridge in the US

w: What began as a parish founded in 1921 became the cathedral seat of the newly created Diocese of Memphis fifty years later, when the church built in 1938 was elevated to Immaculate Conception Cathedral. A 2001 renovation kept the building current without erasing its early-20th-century bones.
s: Seat of the Diocese of Memphis since 1971
_facts: Parish founded 1921
Church building constructed 1938
Became cathedral when the Diocese of Memphis was erected in 1971
Major renovation in 2001

w: Founded by artist-blacksmith James Wallace, this is one of the only museums in the country devoted entirely to metalwork - forged gates, sculpture, tools, and the smiths who made them. Exhibitions rotate through fine metalsmithing alongside public programs that keep the actual craft, not just its history, alive.
s: A museum built by a blacksmith, for blacksmiths
_facts: Founded by artist-blacksmith James Wallace
Formerly called the National Ornamental Metal Museum
Devoted to exhibitions of metalwork and public metalsmithing programs

w: Built in 1991 as a 20,142-seat arena echoing Memphis's Egyptian namesake, this steel-and-glass pyramid ranks among the ten tallest ever built anywhere. It sat dark after 2007 until Bass Pro Shops moved in in 2015, filling it with a megastore, a hotel, a bowling alley, and an archery range under one very literal roof.
s: A 32-story pyramid, now selling fishing rods
_facts: Built 1991 as a 20,142-seat arena on the Mississippi riverbank
321 ft tall, base sides 591 ft; among the ten tallest pyramids in the world
Unused as an arena after 2007
Reopened 2015 as a Bass Pro Shops megastore with hotel, restaurants, bowling alley, archery range, and a waterfowl museum

w: This museum complex is built around the former Lorraine Motel, where Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated in 1968, and traces the civil rights movement from the 17th century to the present. Reopened in 2014 with expanded multimedia exhibits, it became a Smithsonian affiliate museum in 2016.
s: Built around the Lorraine Motel, where King died
_facts: Built around the former Lorraine Motel, site of MLK Jr.'s 1968 assassination
Traces US civil rights history from the 17th century to present
Reopened 2014 after renovation with more multimedia/interactive displays
Smithsonian affiliate since 2016

w: Running 1.8 miles from the Mississippi to East Street, Beale Street has carried Memphis's musical identity for more than a century, its clubs and storefronts entwined with the history of the blues itself. Today's crowds come for the same reason they always did: live music spilling out of open doors.
s: The street where Memphis blues took shape
_facts: Runs about 1.8 miles from the Mississippi River to East Street
Significant in the history of blues music
Blues clubs and restaurants are major tourist draws today
Hosts festivals and outdoor concerts

w: Opened in 1982 to ferry visitors across Wolf River Harbor to the Mud Island entertainment park, this suspended monorail dangled below a footbridge for decades before age caught up with it. Multiple breakdowns through 2018 - including one bad enough to call in the fire department - finally grounded the motor for good.
s: A monorail to Mud Island that kept breaking down
_facts: Opened July 3, 1982, connecting downtown Memphis to Mud Island
Suspended monorail beneath a footbridge over Wolf River Harbor
Multiple malfunctions in 2018, including a fire-department rescue of stranded passengers
Motor ultimately failed

w: Opened in 1925 in downtown Memphis, the Peabody built its whole identity around a twice-daily ritual: the "Peabody Ducks" waddle out of a rooftop home, ride the elevator down, and march across a red carpet into the lobby fountain, then reverse the trip come evening. A century on, the march still stops foot traffic.
s: The hotel where ducks commute to the lobby
_facts: Historic luxury hotel opened 1925
Known for the "Peabody Ducks" that live on the rooftop and march to the lobby fountain daily
Member of Historic Hotels of America

w: Sitting on the corner of Main and Beale, this National Register theater has hosted everything from vaudeville circuits to touring Broadway shows across its 2,308 seats. Paired with the adjoining Halloran Centre, it's run as a nonprofit that mixes performance with education.
s: A 2,308-seat vaudeville palace on Beale Street
_facts: 2,308-seat venue on the National Register of Historic Places
Located at the intersection of South Main and Beale streets
Paired with the Halloran Centre for Performing Arts & Education
Run by the nonprofit Orpheum Theatre Group, which also runs education programs

w: Established in 1906 in Midtown Memphis, Overton Park packs an art museum, a zoo, a nine-hole golf course, and a lake onto 342 acres - but its real rarity is the Old Forest, a stand of old-growth woodland that's one of the few left standing anywhere in Tennessee. Long walks under trees older than the park itself.
s: 342 acres holding one of Tennessee's last old forests
_facts: 342-acre public park, established 1906
Contains the Memphis Brooks Museum of Art, Memphis Zoo, 9-hole golf course, Rainbow Lake
Home to the Old Forest Arboretum, one of the few remaining old-growth forests in Tennessee

n: Belz Museum of Asian and Judaic Art
w: Opened in 1998 from the private collection of Memphis developers Jack and Marilyn Belz, this downtown museum pairs Qing-dynasty jade and tapestries with Judaic art under one roof - an unusual combination born from one couple's decades of collecting. Over a thousand objects, one shared home.
_facts: Opened 1998 as the Peabody Place Museum, renamed 2007
Based on the private collection of Jack and Marilyn Belz
Over 1,000 objects including jade, tapestries, furniture, carvings
Notable Qing dynasty holdings
